Threshingfloor
þHRESH-ing-flor
n.
Threshing + floor; the flat, open, often elevated surface where grain was beaten or trampled to separate the wheat from the chaff. Hebrew gōren; Greek halōn. Biblically significant for several major events: Araunah’s threshingfloor (the temple site), Ruth’s threshingfloor scene, John the Baptist’s eschatological-threshing imagery.

Biblical Definition

The threshingfloor was the flat, open, often elevated surface (typically a stone platform on a hill where the wind could carry away the chaff) on which the harvested grain was beaten or trampled to separate the kernels of wheat from the surrounding chaff and straw. The biblical threshingfloor appears in several theologically loaded narratives. First, Araunah’s threshingfloor as the site of the future temple. 2 Samuel 24 records David’s sin of numbering Israel without the atonement-payment, the resulting plague that swept across the kingdom, and the LORD’s instruction through the prophet Gad for David to build an altar on the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite. David’s response is one of the great expressions of substantive worship: nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing (2 Sam 24:24). He paid Araunah 50 shekels of silver for the threshingfloor and the oxen, built the altar, offered the sacrifices, and the LORD was entreated for the land and stayed the plague. 1 Chronicles 21 records the parallel account; 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies this very threshingfloor (the threshingfloor of Ornan / Araunah the Jebusite on Mount Moriah) as the site Solomon later chose for the temple. The threshingfloor that was the place of plague-stopping atonement-sacrifice became the place of the perpetual temple-worship. Second, Ruth’s threshingfloor scene. Ruth 3 records the climactic encounter between Ruth and Boaz at the threshingfloor where Boaz was winnowing barley. Following Naomi’s instructions, Ruth approaches Boaz at night on the threshingfloor and appeals to him as her kinsman-redeemer. The threshingfloor becomes the setting of one of Scripture’s great romance-and-redemption scenes, with Boaz pledging to perform the kinsman-redeemer role and the narrative moving toward the marriage that produces Obed, the grandfather of David and ancestor of Christ. Third, the eschatological-threshing imagery. John the Baptist’s preaching used threshingfloor-imagery to describe Christ’s coming judgment: whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt 3:12; Luke 3:17). The threshingfloor here is the eschatological field where Christ will separate the wheat (the genuine saints) from the chaff (the unrepentant), gathering the wheat into the heavenly garner and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire. The biblical threshingfloor therefore carries substantial theological substance across its various uses: the temple-site secured by David’s costly worship and atonement-sacrifice; the setting of redemption in the Ruth-and-Boaz narrative; the eschatological imagery of Christ’s coming judgment that will separate wheat from chaff. The contemporary believer who encounters the threshingfloor in his Bible reading does well to attend to its substantive use: it is no mere agricultural setting but the location of plague-stopping sacrifice, redemptive providence, and the prophetic image of the day of the Lord’s separating judgment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines THRESHING-FLOOR as a place or floor of earth, on which grain is beaten out; in scripture, the threshingfloor of Araunah which became the temple-site (2 Sam 24; 2 Chr 3:1), the setting of Ruth’s appeal to Boaz as kinsman-redeemer (Ruth 3), and John the Baptist’s eschatological imagery for Christ’s coming separation of wheat from chaff (Matt 3:12).

THRESHING-FLOOR, n. — A place or floor of earth or stone, on which grain is beaten out; usually elevated, in a position exposed to the wind for the winnowing-separation of chaff from grain.

THRESH, v.t. — To beat out grain from the husk; to separate the corn from the chaff by striking or by trampling, often with oxen.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 24:24 — "And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver."

2 Chronicles 3:1 — "Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite."

Ruth 3:6-7 — "And she went down unto the floor, and did according to all that her mother in law bade her. And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of corn..."

Matthew 3:12 — "Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire."

Modern Corruption

The threshingfloor doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the general loss of attention to biblical-agricultural-setting detail in much contemporary preaching, which misses the substantive theological substance the various threshingfloor-references carry—the temple-site grounded in costly worship, the redemption-narrative setting, and the eschatological-separation imagery of Christ’s coming judgment.

expand to see more

Contemporary preaching often skips the biblical-agricultural-setting details as quaint background to the narrative without operative theological substance. The threshingfloor-references particularly carry substantial substance that the missing-the-setting-detail corruption obscures. David’s purchase of Araunah’s threshingfloor at full price, his refusal to offer burnt offerings of what cost him nothing, and his expressed principle (I will surely buy it of thee at a price) is one of the great OT teachings on the costliness of true worship. The 50 shekels paid for the threshingfloor (and the corresponding 600 shekels of gold for the entire site mentioned in 1 Chr 21:25) anchored the very location of the future temple in the principle of costly worship; Solomon’s temple was built on a site secured by David’s explicit refusal of free worship. The pastoral application is direct: true worship costs something; the worship that costs nothing is not the worship the LORD accepts. The recovery is the recovery of attention to the substantive details of the OT narrative, including the threshingfloor settings that carry their own theological weight.

The eschatological-threshing imagery in John the Baptist’s preaching (Matt 3:12; Luke 3:17) is perhaps the most pastorally substantive of the threshingfloor uses. Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. The image is precise. Christ comes to the threshingfloor of the world; His winnowing-fan is in His hand; He will separate the wheat (the genuine saints) from the chaff (the unrepentant); the wheat is gathered into the heavenly garner; the chaff is burned with unquenchable fire. The contemporary preaching that softens this eschatological-judgment language has often muted what John the Baptist explicitly proclaimed as part of the Christ’s coming work. The recovery is the recovery of John’s actual proclamation: Christ is the wheat-and-chaff-separating Judge who comes; the call is to be genuine wheat now, lest one be found chaff at the threshingfloor of His judgment. The threshingfloor-doctrine therefore organizes both the costly-worship principle (Araunah’s purchase) and the eschatological-judgment warning (John’s preaching), with the redemptive-narrative substance of the Ruth-and-Boaz scene weaving redemption-providence into the same setting. The contemporary preacher who skips the agricultural-setting details misses substantive doctrinal content the biblical writers deliberately included.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gōren (threshingfloor) and Greek halōn (threshingfloor); the flat, often elevated stone-platform on which grain was beaten and winnowed; biblically significant in the Araunah threshingfloor as the temple-site secured by David’s costly worship (2 Sam 24; 2 Chr 3:1), the Ruth-and-Boaz redemption-narrative (Ruth 3), and John the Baptist’s eschatological-separation imagery for Christ’s coming judgment (Matt 3:12).

Hebrew gōren (H1637) — threshingfloor (over 30 OT uses).

Greek halōn (G257) — threshingfloor (Matt 3:12; Luke 3:17, the only NT uses).

Hebrew dūsh (H1758) — to thresh (the verb).

Greek ptuon (G4425) — winnowing-fan (Matt 3:12; Luke 3:17, the separator-tool used on the threshingfloor).
